topics.title: What is OOP?
topics.learn: OOP is a programming paradigm based on objects and classes. Objects contain data and code that operates on that data. OOP can also be understood as designing software using real-world entities such as Car, Student, and Account.
topics.example: A Car object can contain properties such as color and engine information and behaviors such as drive and brake.

topics.title: Need of OOP
topics.learn: OOP addresses problems such as unclear modular structure, poor code reuse, insecure data access, difficulty managing large programs, and difficulty modelling real-world entities.
topics.example: Classes group data and logic, while inheritance enables code reuse.

topics.title: Advantages of OOP
topics.learn: The notes identify modularity, reusability, data hiding, maintainability, real-world modelling, and scalability as advantages of OOP.
topics.example: A large application can be divided into classes so individual parts can be changed more easily.

topics.title: Class
topics.learn: A class is the blueprint or template defining the structure and behavior of objects.
topics.example: A Car class can define color, engineCC, and drive().

topics.title: Object
topics.learn: An object is a real-world entity or instance of a class. It contains characteristics and behaviors defined by the class.
topics.example: A particular red car created from the Car class is an object.

topics.title: Class vs Object
topics.learn: A class is the blueprint, while an object is an actual instance of that blueprint created in memory and used for operations.
topics.example: Car is the class and a particular car is the object.

topics.title: Access Specifiers / Modifiers
topics.learn: Access specifiers define the visibility or access level of class members. The notes cover private, protected, and public.
topics.example: Private members are accessible inside the class, protected members inside the class and derived classes, and public members broadly.

topics.title: Friend Class
topics.learn: A C++ friend class is granted special access to private and protected members of another class.
topics.example: A Mechanic class can access a private engine number of Car when declared as a friend.

topics.title: Encapsulation
topics.learn: Encapsulation wraps data and methods into one unit called a class and supports data hiding through private access.
topics.example: A class hides internal data and exposes it through methods.

topics.title: Inheritance
topics.learn: Inheritance allows a child or derived class to inherit properties and behaviors from a parent or base class.
topics.example: Car inherits start() from Vehicle.

topics.title: Polymorphism
topics.learn: Polymorphism is the ability of objects to take different forms or behave differently depending on context.
topics.example: The same person behaves differently as a student, player, passenger, or child.

topics.title: Abstraction
topics.learn: Abstraction hides unnecessary details and shows only relevant features.
topics.example: A smartphone user can use applications without knowing their internal implementation.

topics.title: Encapsulation & Data Hiding
topics.learn: Encapsulation combines attributes and methods into a class while restricting direct access to internal data.
topics.example: Student.age is private and accessed using setAge() and getAge().

topics.title: Constructor Basics
topics.learn: A constructor is a special method automatically invoked when an object is created and is used to initialize the object.
topics.example: Student() initializes a Student object.

topics.title: Default / Non-Parameterized Constructor
topics.learn: A non-parameterized or default constructor has no parameters.
topics.example: Student() { }

topics.title: Parameterized Constructor
topics.learn: A parameterized constructor accepts values to initialize object attributes during creation.
topics.example: Student(string name) initializes name.

topics.title: Copy Constructor
topics.learn: A copy constructor creates a new object as a copy of an existing object.
topics.example: Student(const Student &s) copies data from another Student.

topics.title: Destructor in C++
topics.learn: A destructor is automatically called when an object goes out of scope or is explicitly deleted. It is used to free resources.
topics.example: ~Student() is called when the Student object leaves its scope.

topics.title: Java Garbage Collection
topics.learn: Java does not use destructors in the manner described for C++. Instead, garbage collection automatically handles memory occupied by objects that are no longer in use.
topics.example: The garbage collector identifies unreachable objects and reclaims their memory.

topics.title: Scope Resolution Operator (::)
topics.learn: The C++ scope resolution operator is used to access members outside the current scope or members belonging to a specific class or namespace.
topics.example: Student::show() defines a class member function outside the class.

topics.title: this Pointer
topics.learn: The this keyword refers to the current object. The notes describe it as a pointer in C++ and a reference in Java.
topics.example: C++ uses this->name while Java uses this.name.

topics.title: Shallow Copy
topics.learn: A shallow copy copies the reference or address of dynamic members. Both objects can therefore share the same memory.
topics.example: Changing s2.marks can also change s1.marks when both refer to the same memory.

topics.title: Deep Copy
topics.learn: A deep copy creates new memory and copies the actual value, making the copied objects independent.
topics.example: Changing s2.marks does not affect s1.marks after a proper deep copy.

topics.title: Shallow vs Deep Copy
topics.learn: The key difference is whether dynamic data is shared or independently copied.
topics.example: Shallow copy shares the referenced memory; deep copy creates independent storage.

topics.title: Inheritance Basics
topics.learn: Inheritance allows a child or derived class to inherit properties and behaviors from a parent or base class.
topics.example: Car derives from Vehicle and inherits start().

topics.title: Modes of Inheritance
topics.learn: C++ supports public, protected, and private inheritance modes, which determine how inherited base members are treated in the derived class.
topics.example: class Derived : public Base

topics.title: Single Inheritance
topics.learn: One derived class inherits from one base class.
topics.example: A → B

topics.title: Multilevel Inheritance
topics.learn: A class is derived from a class that is already derived from another class.
topics.example: A → B → C

topics.title: Hierarchical Inheritance
topics.learn: Multiple classes inherit from a single base class.
topics.example: B and C both inherit from A.

topics.title: Multiple Inheritance
topics.learn: A class inherits from two or more base classes. The notes state that C++ supports this directly, while Java supports multiple inheritance through interfaces.
topics.example: class C : public A, public B

topics.title: Hybrid Inheritance
topics.learn: Hybrid inheritance combines two or more types of inheritance.
topics.example: A combination of multiple and multilevel inheritance.

topics.title: Diamond Problem
topics.learn: The diamond problem occurs in multiple inheritance when two classes share a common base and another class inherits from both, creating ambiguity.
topics.example: D inherits from B and C, while B and C both inherit from A.

topics.title: Virtual Inheritance
topics.learn: C++ virtual inheritance ensures only one copy of a shared base class is inherited and prevents the diamond problem.
topics.example: class B : virtual public A

topics.title: Java's Approach
topics.learn: Java does not allow multiple inheritance through classes, so the classic diamond problem does not occur with classes. Java uses interfaces.
topics.example: A class can implement multiple interfaces and provide the required behavior.

topics.title: Polymorphism
topics.learn: Polymorphism means many forms and allows objects or methods to behave differently in different contexts.
topics.example: Animal references can represent different derived objects such as Dog or Cat.

topics.title: Compile-time Polymorphism
topics.learn: Compile-time or static polymorphism is resolved at compile time. The notes cover method overloading and C++ operator overloading.
topics.example: add(int,int) and add(int,int,int).

topics.title: Runtime Polymorphism
topics.learn: Runtime or dynamic polymorphism determines the method to execute at runtime based on the actual object type.
topics.example: A base pointer referencing a Dog can call Dog's overridden speak().

topics.title: Overloading vs Overriding
topics.learn: Overloading uses the same method name with different parameters, while overriding provides a derived implementation of a base method with the matching signature.
topics.example: add(int,int) vs a derived class overriding speak().

topics.title: Virtual Functions
topics.learn: A C++ virtual function enables runtime binding so the correct derived implementation is selected through a base pointer or reference.
topics.example: Animal* a = new Dog(); a->speak();

topics.title: Abstraction
topics.learn: Abstraction hides unnecessary or internal implementation details and shows only relevant or essential features.
topics.example: A smartphone user interacts with applications without seeing their internal implementation.

topics.title: Pure Virtual Function
topics.learn: A C++ pure virtual function has no implementation in the base class and is declared using = 0.
topics.example: virtual void area() = 0;

topics.title: Abstract Class in C++
topics.learn: A C++ class containing at least one pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated.
topics.example: Shape with virtual void area() = 0.

topics.title: Abstract Class in Java
topics.learn: A Java abstract class cannot be instantiated and can contain abstract methods, concrete methods, fields, constructors, and access modifiers.
topics.example: Animal can contain an abstract makeSound() and a concrete sleep().

topics.title: Interface in Java
topics.learn: An interface is a contract defining what a class must do. The notes include abstract methods, default methods, and static methods.
topics.example: Flyable can define fly(), land(), and info().

topics.title: Abstract Class vs Interface
topics.learn: The notes compare inheritance, constructors, fields, concrete methods, access modifiers, instantiation, use case, and multiple inheritance support.
topics.example: Abstract classes can provide shared base logic while interfaces declare capabilities or behaviors.

topics.title: Static Data Member
topics.learn: A static data member is shared by all objects of a class and is allocated only once.
topics.example: static int count;

topics.title: Static Member Function
topics.learn: A static member function belongs to the class rather than an object, can be called without an object, and can directly access static members.
topics.example: ClassName::showCount() in C++.
